title: Self-growing Cu/Sn Bimetallic Electrocatalysts on Nitrogen-Doped Porous Carbon Cloth with 3D-Hierarchical Honeycomb Structure for Highly Active Carbon Dioxide Reduction
abstract: The electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) into liquid fuels is a promising avenue to both store intermittent renewable energy and reduce global CO2 emission, but daunting bottlenecks owing to poor selectivity, low activity and stability of the electrocatalysts. Herein, we report that bimetallic copper and tin are simultaneously deposited on the nitrogen doped porous carbon cloth (N-CC) via an efficient and facile co-electroplating strategy. The highly conductive N-doped porous carbon cloth as substrate enables a largely uniform distribution of N-doped defects, which can provide more active sites for the nucleation and growth of anchoring nano-sized Cn/Sn (3.39nm). The as-prepared electrode (Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC), with a 3D-hierarchical porous honeycomb structure, could not only favor the diffusion of electrolyte and serve as “transfer posts” to confine the intermediates of reduced CO2, but also provide abundant terrace, ledge and kink atoms to function as active site for highly efficient CO2RR. As such, the obtained Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC electrode convert CO2 to formate with allured faradic efficiency (90.24 %), partial current density (15.56 mA cm) and production rate (173 μmol h cm) at -0.97 VRHE, along with a long-term tolerance in CO2RR. This study may provide a new design for self-growing bimetallic catalyst on N-doped porous substrate to regulate advanced catalysts/electrodes for different applications.

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
The electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) into liquid fuels is a promising avenue to both store intermittent renewable energy and reduce global CO2 emission, but daunting bottlenecks owing to poor selectivity, low activity and stability of the electrocatalysts. Herein, we report that bimetallic copper and tin are simultaneously deposited on the nitrogen doped porous carbon cloth (N-CC) via an efficient and facile co-electroplating strategy. The highly conductive N-doped porous carbon cloth as substrate enables a largely uniform distribution of N-doped defects, which can provide more active sites for the nucleation and growth of anchoring nano-sized Cn/Sn (3.39nm). The as-prepared electrode (Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC), with a 3D-hierarchical porous honeycomb structure, could not only favor the diffusion of electrolyte and serve as “transfer posts” to confine the intermediates of reduced CO2, but also provide abundant terrace, ledge and kink atoms to function as active site for highly efficient CO2RR. As such, the obtained Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC electrode convert CO2 to formate with allured faradic efficiency (90.24 %), partial current density (15.56 mA cm-2) and production rate (173 μmol h-1 cm-2) at -0.97 VRHE, along with a long-term tolerance in CO2RR. This study may provide a new design for self-growing bimetallic catalyst on N-doped porous substrate to regulate advanced catalysts/electrodes for different applications.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Environmental pollution and energy crisis as one of the greatest challenges have
caused widespread concern[1]. The electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) to fuels and chemicals is attributed to be a potential way to alleviate environmental problems (global warming and climate change) and store intermittent renewable energy (wind and solar power)[2]. However, the techno economic viability of directly converting CO2 into hydrocarbons requires to develop highly selective, active and durable electrocatalyst in this process[3]. In the meantime, although a multitude of possible CO2 RR products have been experimentally identified, and more desirable to steer the selectivity toward C2+ products owing to their higher industrial values, the high catalytic efficiencies and production rates for C1 products (e.g., CO, HCOOH and/or formate) offer more immediate opportunities for the commercial-scale applications of CO2RR. Specifically, formate with economically viable property and, as a significant hydrogen carrier with high energy density could have a promising application in formic acid fuel cells[4].
Many recent studies have reported that Bi[3],Cu[5], In[6], Sn[7] and Co[8] as
electrocatalyst could reduce CO2 into formate, howbeit the high overpotential and inferior durability are two important aspects that cannot be neglected in evaluating the performance of these catalysts[9,10]. Cu-based catalysts with high activity have a potential to produce multiple hydrocarbons, like carbon monoxide[11], formate[12], methane[13], ethylene[14] and ethanol, etc.[15]. As yet, both polycrystalline copper and single crystal copper show poor selectivity[16] and low faradic efficiencies (FE) of
target product below 65%[12]. On the other hand, Sn-based catalysts have been widely

recognized to possess high selectivity for CO2RR to formate with FE in exceeding 80%[17], unfortunately, the activity of tin catalysts is still far from practical application owing to the low current density usually less than 15 mA cm-2 even in a high overpotential[18]. Hence, how to optimize the selectivity and FE of copper electrode and how to enhance the activity of tin electrode is an urgent matter to solve. Considering the benefits of copper and tin in the process of CO2RR, numerous efforts have been devoted to modulating the catalysts’ morphology[19], crystal structure[20] and composition of copper and tin[4] with the purpose to optimize the selectivity, activity and durability of catalysts.
It is noteworthy that, in addition to electrocatalysts engineering, the conventional
electrode is realized by mixing the as-prepared copper and tin catalyst with polymeric binders and extra conductive additives as ink, and then coated on a carbon substrate[21]. This strategy usually results in limited active surface areas, undesired microstructures, a large amount of dead volumes, uncontrolled interface that are unfavorable for multiphase reactant/product mass transport and electron conductance[22]. Electroplating method has actually attracted lots of attention due to its convenience and innocuity[4]. The most attracting point is that metal or alloy can be directly deposited on the substrate (carbon paper[10], copper foil[19] or carbon cloth[23,24]) by electrochemical reaction, which can be called as one-step synthesis of self-growing electrode. Unfortunately, when it comes to copper and tin, the direct preparation of its bimetallic nanostructures with self-growing electrode is still challenging. To the best of our knowledge, recent progresses in electrodeposition are made to fabricate copper and tin electrode for CO2RR mainly by two-step methods: (i) the growth of copper atom on the carbon substrate or the Jo ur na l P re -p
ro of
pretreatment of copper substrate, (ii) electrodeposited tin on the modified copper substrate [19,25-27]. Although this method shows a good performance of CO2RR, there are too many uncertain factors in the repetitive work due to one more step compositions. One way to solve these problems is the simultaneous introduction of alloy of copper and tin, which is favorable for the fine-regulating of the crystal phase and nano-micro morphology by engineering the synthetic condition of alloy[28]. Thus, self-growing Cu/Sn bimetallic electrocatalysts via a convenient and time-efficient preparation procedure have shown a promising protocol for converting CO2 to fuels.
Herein, we propose an effective and facile protocol to synthesize copper and tin alloy
catalysts on N-doped porous carbon cloth by using a co-electrodeposition strategy (Fig. 1a). The as-prepared Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC electrode, with a 3D-hierarchical porous honeycomb structure, could not only favor the diffusion of electrolyte and serve as “transfer posts” to confine the intermediates of reduced CO2, but also provide abundant terrace, ledge and kink atoms to function as active site for highly efficient CO2RR. Under these circumstances, CO2 with the electrolyte flowing in could diffuse into this porous structure, and the productions with the electrolyte flowing out could simultaneously be transported out of these channels. Besides, the highly conductive N-doped graphitic carbon cloth (CC) could easily allow fast electron penetration between the interface of CC and metals, which therefore favors the formation of CO2*- intermediate from the electron transfer of CO2.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text:
Carbon cloth (CC) was purchased from Phychemi (HK) Limited Company. Tin (II)
chloride dihydrate (SnCl2 2H2O, ≥98%), Copper (II) chloride dihydrate (CuCl2 2H2O, ≥98%), Trisodium citrate dehydrate (Na3C6H5O7 2H2O, ≥99%), Urea (CH4N2O, ≥99%) and Potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3, ≥99.5%) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. sections.heading: 2.2.1. Preparation of porous N-doped CC
sections.text:
The raw CC was cleaned by ultrasonication in 0.1 M HCl, ethanol, deionized water
for 30 min sequentially. The cleaned CC was transferred to saturated urea solution for the next 1 h physical deposition, and thereafter curdled in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 3 h. The CC covered with urea crystal was calcined at 550oC in an air condition for 3 h at a heating rate of 5°C min–1. The obtained porous N-doped CC (N-CC) was used as substrate to co-electroplate Cu/Sn, as explicitly described in section 2.2.2. Compared to the raw CC in Fig. 2a, N-CC has a largely uniform distribution of N-doped defects in Fig. 2b, which can provide more active sites for the nucleation and growth of anchoring nanosized Cu/Sn[29]. sections.heading: 2.2.2. Fabrication of Cu/Sn electrode
sections.text:
Cu/Sn was co-electrodeposited onto the as-prepared porous N-CC in a compartment
with a three-electrode configuration. A spectral graphite carbon wire was used as the counter electrode and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) was applied as the reference electrode. Considering Sn2+/Sn (LSV Sn) couple has a more negative reduction potential than Cu2+/Cu (LSV Cu) couple (Fig. S1), the chosen constant potential to successfully co-electroplate Cu/Sn should make sure that Cu2+ and Sn2+ could be simultaneously evolved from electroplate liquid (LSV CuSn). Key to the co-electroplating Cu/Sn was applied at -0.75 V vs SCE due to the intersection of three LSVs, while the depositing time was prolonged to 6h below 20oC in order that the N-CC was fully wrapped by Cu/Sn. The plating solution contains different molar ratio of SnCl2 2H2O and CuCl2 2H2O in total 0.02 M, 0.1 M Na3C6H5O7 2H2O and 0.1 M CH4N2O. The obtained electrodes are denoted as Cu-N-CC, Cu(1)Sn(1)-N-CC, Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC, Cu(1)Sn(9)-N-CC, Sn-N-CC according to the molar ratio of Cu2+ and Sn2+ in plating solution, respectively.

sections.text:
The surface morphology and element distribution of as-prepared Cu(x)Sn(y)-N-CC
electrode were analyzed by a S-4800 field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) operating at 5 kV. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analyses were performed at a high-resolution Hitachi JEM-2100F operating at 200 kV to obtain information of the average particle size as well as the distribution of the as-prepared Cu/Sn electrocatalysts, while the element distribution of these particles was determined on a molybdenum wire
mesh by means of energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) attached to transmission

sections.heading: 2.3. Electrochemical measurement
sections.text:
The electrochemical performance of CO2 reduction reaction was tested by CHI 660E
electrochemical workstation (CH Instruments) in H-type reactor with a three-electrode system, where Cu(x)Sn(y)-CC-CN was used as working electrode and Ag/AgCl was applied as reference electrode, 20% IrO2 coated on the carbon paper was employed as counter electrode for oxygen evolution reaction (OER). A 0.5 M KOH solution was conducted as anolyte and KHCO3 with different concentrations was conducted as catholyte, wherein anode and cathode were separated by a basic anion (OH-) exchange FAD membrane (Germen). The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed by AC impedance mode over a 0.5 to 100 kHz at -0.97 V vs RHE. Without further specification, the potential mentioned below will be relative to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). The catalytic performance and stability of CO2 reduction were conducted by applying the amperometric i-t curve mode. sections.heading: 3.1. Characterization and formation mechanisms of Cu(x)Sn(y)-N-CC electrode
sections.text:
As illustrated in Fig. 1b, the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the as-prepared
five samples were analyzed to provide evidences of their crystal phases. Cu-N-CC shows the typical crystallographic state with three strong shoulder peaks at 43.39o, 50.43o, 74.13o, which correspond to the (111), (200), and (220) crystal facets of metal Cu (JCPDS PDF# 04-0836). The main diffraction peaks of Sn-N-CC at 30.64o, 32.02o, 43.87o, 44.91o, 79.47o indicate the (200), (101), (220), (211), (312) planes of metal Sn (JCPDS PDF# 04-0673), respectively. Interestingly, the XRD patterns of Cu(1)Sn(1)-N-CC, Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC, Cu(1)Sn(9)-N-CC are quite different from Cu-N-CC and Sn-N-CC[28]. The intensity of Cu (111) and (200) is obviously weakened with the addition of Sn2+ into the plating solution, indicating the formation of Cu/Sn alloy and the presence of crystalline alloy phases. Noticeably, by introducing the Sn2+ molar content as same as Cu2+ in plating solution, there are only two main diffraction peaks of Cu(1)Sn(1)-N-CC in accordance with Cu41Sn11 (660) (JCPDS PDF# 30-0510) plane and Cu (111) plane. Thereinto, the intensity of Cu41Sn11 (660) is higher than Cu (111) in Fig. S2, implying that Cu41Sn11 is more likely to be formed than crystallographic Cu. However, with Sn2+ and Cu2+ molar ratio reaching to 4:1, it is surprising to observe that the dominant diffraction peak of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC becomes Cu6.25Sn5 (110) (JCPDS PDF# 47-1575), and Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC also exhibits the weaker intensity of Sn (220) and (221) planes, which can be deemed as the saturation of Sn2+ around growth substrate (CC). Moreover, when such molar ratio of Sn2+ and Cu2+ raising to 9:1, Sn2+ might have a priority to get J ur na l P re -p ro of
electrons to be reduced possibly through substituting the Cu2+ reduction sites[30], which can be demonstrated by the more appearance of Sn (220) and (221) planes in Cu(1)Sn(9)N-CC than Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC.
The valance state and elemental composition of CC and N-CC were investigated by
XPS analysis as depicted in Fig. 1c and Fig. S3, confirming the existence of C, O and N elements in N-CC, which can be further approved by SEM mapping results of those elements in Fig. 2b and Table. S1. The XPS C 1s spectra of N-CC exhibits three main asymmetrical peaks at 284.75 eV, 285.40 eV, 286.30 eV, attributing to C-C, C-O or C=O, C=N[31], respectively. Therefore, the presence of C=N can indicate that N atoms have been successfully introduced into carbon cloth matrix.
The oxidation states of Sn 3d and Cu 2p in the Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC before and after
CO2RR were analyzed by XPS measurements, as shown in Fig. 1d-g. Significantly, the Sn 3d for Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC before and after CO2RR exhibits similar states at 484.70 eV and 493.05 eV corresponding to Sn(0) species, likewise at 486.50 eV and 494.90 eV ascribing to Sn(II) species, which may be attributed to an air-oxidized Sn surface under air condition. The peak position of Sn 3d before and after CO2RR has almost no changed, suggesting no emergence of other new states. Nevertheless, the proportion of Sn(II) and Sn(0) increases from 7.45:1 to 9.24:1 calculated by the area of those peaks. The increment of Sn(II) content might be deemed as the changes of morphology during electrolysis, further illustration thereof is in the stability test.
The Cu 2p XPS spectra are very hard to identify because Cu(0) and Cu(I) have very
close binding energy values at 932.6 eV and 932.9 eV. The peak positions of Cu 2p before and after CO2RR are observed at 932.10 eV and 952.00 eV assigning to Cu(0)/(I)
Jo ur
na l P
re -p

and at 934.20 eV and 954.30 eV ascribing to Cu(II)[32]. The proportion of Cu(0)/(I) and Cu(II) shows the similar trend of Sn(0) and Sn(II), with the ratio increasing from 6.76:1 to 12.9:1. It is worth noting that the oxidized states of Cu and Sn species might owe to the exposure of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC in 0.5 M CO2 saturated KHCO3 under nearly neutral pH, or on the flip side the subsequent exposure in the air when transferring the Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC to test the surface spectroscopy[25].
The microstructure and morphology of the as-synthesized Cu(x)Sn(y)-N-CC electrode
were studied by SEM images. As shown in Fig. 2c-g and Fig. S4, the particle size, surface shape and architecture of different samples do distinctly alter by adjusting the atom ratio of Cu and Sn. Except for the discrepancy from microscopic level, the difference of Cu(x)Sn(y)-N-CC can also be readily distinguished from macroscopic level in Fig. S5. It can be observed that the Cu-N-CC electrode shows much more fine particles on the compact surface with a tight structure (Fig. 2c), whereas the Sn-N-CC electrode manifests a large plain with some tiny seeds scattering on the surface (Fig. 2f). In comparison with Cu-N-CC and Sn-N-CC, however, the as-obtained Cu(1)Sn(1)-N-CC displays the distinctly different morphology with numerous conjunctions of micro blocks (Fig. 2d). This may be the reason from the synergistic effect of Cu2+ and Sn2+ around the growth substrate, since the proportion of Cu2+ and Sn2+ in a plating bath does influence the rate of deposition[33]. Cu(1)Sn(9)-N-CC electrode performs the similar microstructure of Sn-N-CC, but alongside the surface edge with evident coverage of highly dispersed fine particles (insert picture of Fig. 2e), same as Cu-N-CC. This may provide evidence that Cu atoms have embedded into the lattice of Sn atoms to form alloy structure. Fig. 2g indicates that Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC, with well geographical distribution of Cu and Sn atoms Jo ur na l P re -p
oo f
(Fig. S6), has a 3D-hierarchical microstructure with some pits combining together on the surface, labyrinthine channels running through different layers and some nano-scale cavities from the inside out. Consequently, various intermediates of reduced CO2 may be stranded in these confined volumes[5], that is, more HCOO- will be generated in this way.
TEM mapping images of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC (Fig. S7) show a better geographical
distribution of well-dispersed Sn and Cu particle with the average size of 3.39 nm (the insert of Fig. 2h), which might be considered the composition of small pits on the surface of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC as shown in Fig. 2g. In this situation, the intimate contact of these nanoparticles is beneficial for interfacial charger transfer. The HRTEM image (the insert of Fig. 2h) reveals that a lattice spacing is 0.2032 nm, corresponding to the (110) plane of Cu6.25Sn5. It is further confirmed by the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns as evident from the distinct ring in Fig. 2i, which is well consistent with the XRD analysis. Additionally, the TEM images of Cu-N-CC are shown in Fig. S8a-b, where some fine particles can be clearly observed matching well with the SEM results. A lattice spacing of 0.2126 nm can be easily found in accordance with the (111) plane of Cu, which can be further validated by the SAED pattern in Fig. S9. In contrast, Fig. S8c exhibits that Cu(1)Sn(1)-N-CC has some nano-sheets, which may be the key components of micro blocks as observed in Fig. 2d. The main exposure crystal facets of those nanosheets are the (111) plane of Cu and (660) plane of Cu41Sn11 corresponding to a lattice spacing of 0.2997 nm (Fig. S8d), and is in consistent with XRD results. As for Cu(1)Sn(9)N-CC and Sn-N-CC (Fig. S10), both of them show the combination of nano-sheets, while Cu(1)Sn(9)-N-CC has better dispersal than Sn-N-CC, which could explain the appearance of micro particles alongside the surface edge as shown in Fig. 2e. The (200) planes of Sn Jo u na l P re -p ro of
can be found in both of two samples (Fig. S10b and d), and SAED patterns (Fig. S11) of Sn has several distinct diffraction rings demonstrating that Sn-N-CC possesses various crystal facets in accordance with XRD results.

sections.heading: 3.2. CO2RR performances of Cu(x)Sn(y)-N-CC electrode
sections.text:
Considering that Cu (Cu2O) and Sn (SnO2) are widely recognized to have good
electrochemical reduction properties of carbon dioxide [5,16,34-37], in order to eliminate the effects of oxidation of the electrode in the air, the as-prepared Cu(x)Sn(y)-N-CC was pretreated at -0.6 V in N2 bubbling 0.5 M KHCO3 by a chronoamperometry method for 30 minutes. Subsequently, linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was tested at 5 mV s-1 under N2 and CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte, separately. In Fig. 3a, Cu(1)Sn(4)-CC-CN electrode shows the onset potential of -0.590 mV at 2 mA cm-1 in CO2 rich condition compared with -0.737 mV in N2 rich condition, implying that the overpotential of the onset potential was reduced 147 mV due to CO2 purged into electrolyte. It is well believed that the onset potential plays an important role in evaluating the overpotential of each electrocatalyst[18], therefore, the great enhancement of current density during CO2 purging compared to N2 should be attributed to the reduction of CO2[38].
To investigate the effects of different electrolytic potential, a potential window
between -0.57 V to -1.07 V was performed as shown in Fig. 3b. It is found that the FEHCOO- of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC keeps continuously increasing with the applied potential reaching a maximum level of 90.24 % at -0.97 V, then maintains > 90% between −1.1 and −0.97 VRHE. Instead, Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC shows the total current density getting larger and larger along with the enhancement of applied potential (Fig. 3c), which might prove
Jo ur

that more CO2 is involved in reduction reaction. This formate selectivity over a broad potential window (−1.1 ～ −0.97 VRHE) and great current density (> 20mA cm-2) on Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC electrode is superior to other known formate-producing CO2RR electrocatalysts (including CuSn NPs/C-A, Cu@Sn nanocones/Cu, and Cu55Sn45 etc.) (see the details in Table S2). For Cu-N-CC (Fig. S12a), the dominant product is H2 despite in CO2-saturated electrolyte, and a small amount of CO and HCOO- can also be detected. This suggests that H2 evolution favors to react in the system of Cu-N-CC as cathode electrode. Moreover, Cu(1)Sn(1)-N-CC and Cu(1)Sn(9)-N-CC (Fig. S12b-c) show the similar trend of the FEHCOO- but no more than 65%, even at the applied potential of - 1.07 V. Apparently, the presence of Cu41Sn11 (660) and Sn (211) according to XRD analysis may function as active planes to catalyze CO2 reduction. Furthermore, Sn-N-CC (Fig. S12d) has a positive effect to produce formate for the CO2RR and a negative effect to depress H2 evolution reaction.

It is generally believed that the mechanism pathway of formate is followed by the
equations (1)-(4), which are vividly depicted in the Fig. 1a. Equation (1) indicates that a CO2 molecule is dissolved in the electrolyte to become an adsorbed CO2 around the electrode[5], and then the adsorbed CO2 obtains an electron (e-) to form CO2*-, while the asterisk represents an active site (Equation (2)). Afterwards, the adsorbed CO2*-
Jo ur
na l P
re -p
ro of
intermediate get the second electron (e-) from the electrode (Equation (3)), and a proton transferring from HCO3- according to the HCO3- = H+ + CO32-. The obtained adsorbed HCOO*− further form formate in the solution (Equation (4)). In Fig. 3d, the Tafel slopes of different catalytic electrodes were performed to illustrate the mechanisms of CO2 reduction. The slope value of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC for formate is 107 mV per decade very close to 118 mV per decade[35], suggesting that the chemical rate-determining step for CO2 reduction is one electron transferring to form an adsorbed CO2*- intermediate (Equation (2))[34,36,39]. As the smaller Tafel slope indicates better catalytic performance of catalyst, the slop values for Cu(1)Sn(1)-N-CC and Cu(1)Sn(9)-N-CC are 1.63 and 1.93 times higher than Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC, implying that the Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC favors mass transport of CO2 reduction intermediate reactant and products[34].
The electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) could reflect the amount of
catalytically active sites. Generally, the ECSA of Cu(x)Sn(y)-N-CC could be measured by electrochemical double layer capacitance (DLC) as depicted in Fig. S13, where the ECSA has a positive relation with double layer capacitance (DLC). The DLC of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC is 3.53 mF, higher than the 3.10 mF of Cu(1)Sn(1)-N-CC, 3.40 mF of SnN-CC and 2.20 mF of Cu(1)Sn(9)-N-CC, except lower than Cu-N-CC, which may be attributed to the copious hydrogen evolution reaction active sites existing on the surface of Cu-N-CC. From the morphology of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC in Fig. 2g, the rough surface, deep ledge and numerous kinks may contain a large number of active sites towards CO2RR, thus the better ECSA of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC is obtained. The Cu-N-CC with high ECSA could result in the increment of charge transfer rate, thus the overall electronic conductivity can be enhanced by the decrease of charge transfer resistance (CTR). As Jo ur na l P
re -p
ro of
shown in Fig. 3e, the CTR of Sn-N-CC is smaller than the other alloy catalytic electrode, demonstrating that copper atoms inserting into the space lattice of tin atoms does influence overall electronic conductivity. In fact, the CTR was found to have a relation of total current density, in which the lower CTR showed a higher total current density (Fig. S14).
Furthermore, the stability of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC is an important parameter to evaluate
the performance of CO2RR in the practical applications. The continuous electrolysis is conducted in CO2 saturated 0.5M KHCO3 for an extended period of time up to 20h. As shown in Fig. 3f, the electrolysis current with a rapid decline in the initial stage is observed at -0.97V, which is attributed to the suppression of hydrogen evolution during the oxide reduction process. After this rapid decrease, the current density keeps almost stable at partial current density of 15.56 mA cm-2. During the first 8h, the FE of formate maintains a platform at 90.24%, which may be believed the higher coverage of the reaction intermediate on the surface of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC driving the production of HCOO-. In the following 12h, the FE of HCOO- has a slight decrease to 84%, the mechanism of FEHCOO- decay could be explained as the following two reasons: (i) from SEM images in inset pictures (Fig. 3f), the surface morphology and structure remain almost unchanged in the first 10h, while at 15h the micro-particles on the surface seem to combine together and at 20h some labyrinthine channels adhere well to become scarred. This could demonstrate that the spectacular morphology and hierarchical structure have a pivotal role in CO2 reduction. (ii) the XPS analysis of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC shows that the content of Cu(0) and Sn(0) would reduce after 20h long-term electrolysis (Fig. 1d-g), which may provide the evidence that the state of metal might influence the production of formate. Jo ur na l P re -p ro f
However, it is unclear whether Cu(0) and Sn(0) were oxidized when they were exposed in the electrolyte functioning as working electrode, or simply by the exposure to air before the measurement of XPS. For underlying the surface states of catalytic electrode during CO2RR, the cyclic voltammogram (CV) was conducted to detect the surface redox potentials of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC in a potential range from -0.64 to 0.93 V, as shown in Fig. S15. The Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC shows two cathodic peaks at 0.48 and 0.31 V due to the reduction of CuO to Cu2O and Cu2O to Cu[16,34], and other two cathodic peaks at -0.20 and -0.50 V corresponding to the reduction of SnO2 to SnO and SnO to Sn, while two anodic peaks at -0.14 and -0.01 V indicating to the oxidation of Sn to SnO and SnO to SnO2[25].
Besides the electrode properties, the concentration of electrolyte did have a marked
impact on the CO2RR of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC. Therefore, different concentrations of KHCO3 were conducted to investigate the production rate and FE of formate. In Fig. S16, the DLC of Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC increases from 2.61mF for 0.1 M saturated CO2 KHCO3 to 4.11 mF for 1 M KHCO3, which can be attributed to the thinner electrical double layer (EDL) in higher concentration of KHCO3[40]. As a matter of fact, the thickness of EDL could be decided by DLC to a certain degree as depicted in Fig. 4a. As shown in Fig. 4b, the CTR (the diameter of the semicircle in Fig. S17) does have a steep decrease of 6.2 Ω from 0.1 M to 0.5 M, and then with a mild decrease of 2.0 Ω from 0.5 M to 1 M, and the solution resistance (the low value in the x-axis of Fig. S17) has the similar decreasing trend with 5.1 Ω from 0.1 M to 0.5 M and 0.7 Ω from 0.5 M to 1 M. These can demonstrate that the former concentration range of KHCO3 has a stronger impact than the latter in CO2RR. The LSV measurements in Fig. 4c reveal that the current density Jo ur na l P
re -p
ro of
increases gradually from 16.1 to 40.83 mA cm-2 at -1.1V. The enhancement of current density along with the increment of KHCO3 concentration can be attributed to the greater ionic conductivity and smaller solution resistance, which may be the main reason to drive the overall electrochemical reaction. As for the production rate of formate, Fig. 4d shows that it starts to increase from 105 μmol h-1 cm-2 in 0.1 M KHCO3, and then hits a plateau at 173 μmol h-1 cm-2 in 0.5 M. Afterwards, it almost keeps smooth from 0.5 M to 1 M, which can be explained by the more H+ accumulating at the electrode surface in the high concentration of KHCO3. The presence of more H+ would promote the formation of formate (Equation (3)), while the formate production rate remains stable beyond 0.5 M KHCO3, implying that the H+ provided by HCO3- is saturated at this point. Besides, a higher total current density can be easily observed in a more concentrated KHCO3, possibly due to the bigger DLC (Fig. 4a) and more ionizing H+ from HCO3-. Additionly, the FE of formate in 0.5M reaches a highest point with a slight decrease in highly concentrated KHCO3, which may be ascribed to the more hydrogen evolution advanced by excess H+ around the electrode.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, by a facile and simple co-electrodeposition of Cu/Sn in a controlled
condition, we have successfully synthesized a 3D-hierarchical honeycomb microstructure of Cu/Sn (3.39nm) nanoparticle highly dispersed on N-doped carbon cloth. The asprepared Cu(1)Sn(4)-N-CC electrode can achieve a high catalytic selective (exceeding 90% over a broad potential window) and activity to electroreduction CO2 to formate with
Jo ur
na l P
re -p
ro of
moderate partial current density and long-term stability (over 20h). Besides, the influence of the concentration of KHCO3 indicated that the production rate of formate reaches to 173 μmol h-1 cm-2 in 0.5 M. FE of formate in 0.5M reached a highest point with a slight decrease in highly concentrated KHCO3. Bimetallic Cu/Sn catalyst through electroplating is a promising way in a scalable preparation for CO2RR, and that grows on the flexible N-doped substrate having a broad scope in the application of flexible device in the future. This study supports a concept that can be extended to develop other bimetallic catalyst for highly stable, efficient and active CO2RR including other energy storage and conversion reactions, such as electroreduction of O2/N2 reaction.
